risks.summary: A bounded context contract has now met real note text; the hand-assembled-declassification gap is closed by type.
risks.detail: NEX-028 caps a context field's value at 200 characters and an envelope at 32 fields, and names fields with stable lowercase identifiers. Every current caller is a test, so none of those bounds has met real note text or a real note title. The first production caller (tool-gateway classification or the approval-recommendation path) is the first genuine test; if a bound is too tight, widening it is a contract change requiring review, not a tweak to a constant. Related honest gap, documented on DecisionRequest.from_context: context_hash is a plain str, so a caller can hand-assemble one, which means taking the declassification decision personally. A later slice can narrow the field to a type only an envelope can construct. UPDATE (NEX-029): ContextEnvelope now has a production caller - the advisory route builds one from a real stored approval record, so the 32-field and 200-char bounds have met real approval data. They have still not met real note text, and context_hash is still a plain str. CLOSED (NEX-030): context_hash is now ContextHash, constructible only through ContextHash._mint, which only ContextEnvelope calls. A caller-assembled string is rejected by decisioning._validate_context_hash. The bounds (32 fields, 200 chars) have still not met real note text - that remains a live observation, not a code gap. CLOSED (NEX-031): the bounds have now met a real stored note body at MAX_CONTENT_BYTES (64 KiB, ~300x the 200-char field cap) and an over-cap record-derived value is withheld rather than raising, so a legal note can no longer deny the advisory. The note-text observation is closed; the stated str.__new__ residual on ContextHash is unchanged and deliberate.

risks.summary: A bounded contract exercised only against a stub has not been exercised against a real provider.
risks.detail: NEX-027 caps a decision's rationale at 400 characters, its confidence/score at [0.0, 1.0], and its choice set at the candidates the caller supplied. The stub adapter always answers at 0.1 confidence with a short rationale, so none of those bounds has met a real vendor payload. The first real adapter is the first genuine test; if it needs a wider rationale or more candidates, that is a contract change requiring review, not a tweak to a constant.

risks.summary: A validity bound written by one clock and read by another gives the wrong answer in both directions.
risks.detail: NEX-026: ApprovalRequest.open stamped expires_at from the caller's Clock port, but the decision path called is_expired, which reads the module wall clock. A request opened on a clock behind the wall clock was judged already lapsed, so a human could not decide a live request; a request opened on a clock ahead of the wall clock was judged still valid after its bound passed, so consent outlived the bound it was granted under. Every existing expiry test used one clock for both open and decide, so the two readings always agreed and the defect was structurally invisible. The repository adapter was already correct, which is why no integration test caught it either. General rule: for every bound, name the clock that writes it and assert the reader uses the same one - and test the disagreement, not just the happy path, because a single-clock suite cannot see this class at all.
risks.status: closed by NEX-026, VERIFIED at b46e2e3

risks.summary: A grant can outlive the consent that justified it, because the grant does not name the consent.
risks.detail: An approval records agent_id and no delegation, so it cannot be attributed to a surviving delegation when one is withdrawn - and nothing withdrew it. RevokeDelegation revoked the delegation and its tokens but left the agent operational, so after re-delegation a token from the new delegation could spend an approval granted under the withdrawn one. RevokeAgent left approvals approved too: latent while the agent check blocks use, but any reactivation path would inherit pre-emergency-stop grants. Closed by NEX-025 on both paths. General rule: for every piece of live authority, ask what revokes it and follow the chain to the end - revoking the container is not enough if the authority is keyed to something that survives it. Same shape as R23 and R26.

risks.summary: A terminal state in one record is not a terminal state in the record that describes the same event.
risks.detail: NEX-023 closed this on the resolve path: InvokeTool commits its ToolInvocation as `started` before entering the handler (correct - a crash must leave a trace), and ResolveInterruptedStep had settled the run without closing that row. NEX-024 found the same defect on the other settle path: AbortAgentRun flipped the run to aborted and never sealed the link, while AgentRun.abort also left a `started` step inside a terminal run. Both halves now settle, in one transaction. General rule, now proven to recur once: any operation that makes a run terminal must settle its mid-flight steps AND seal their invocations in the same transaction. A third settle path reopens this. Two records that disagree are not a partial success.
risks.status: closed on both existing settle paths (resolve: NEX-023; abort: NEX-024)

risks.summary: A field can be persisted, foreign-keyed, and written on every create — and still never be read by the check that needs it.
risks.detail: NEX-022: agent_runs.delegation_id was written by PlanAgentRun on every plan, carried a FK to agent_delegations, and was never consulted by AdvanceAgentRun._load_for_agent, which compared only agent_id. So a token from a different delegation could drive a run, and revoking the planning delegation did not stop it. The schema asserted the binding mattered; the read path disagreed, and nothing failed. General rule: for every security-relevant column, grep for the reads, not just the writes. A column written and never read is either dead or a missing check — decide which, in writing.

risks.summary: A control enforced on every path someone thought of can still miss a path that establishes the same identity.
risks.detail: NEX-006 closed the offboarding gap by calling ensure_tenant_access on the three human identity paths (OIDC callback, session resolution, bearer provider). Agent-token resolution was a fourth way to establish an identity and never called it, so a suspended delegator's agent stayed fully operational for as long as its token lived. The gap survived because the shared seam looked complete: every caller of ensure_tenant_access was correct, and nothing enumerated the callers that were missing. Lesson: when a check is 'the one place', list every identity-establishing path and assert each one calls it, rather than trusting the seam's existence. Closed for agent tokens by 990557d.

risks.summary: A governance gate can be structurally unusable while every test stays green.
risks.detail: NEX-016: human approval was implemented end to end (requests, decisions, expiry, revocation, HTTP routes, 8 tests) yet a durable run could never honour an approval. Two independent defects each alone made resumption impossible: the run failed terminally on the pause, and the unique (agent_id, idempotency_key) constraint was permanently consumed by the denial record. No test covered 'approve, then continue', so the suite was green through a decorative control. The general lesson: a security control needs a test of the full decision-to-effect path, not tests of each half.

risks.summary: A governance record can be unreachable through the API without any error, while the data is intact in storage.
risks.detail: NEX-015: approvals were persisted correctly and list_for_agent existed on the port, but the use case only ever called list_pending_for_agent, so every decided approval was invisible to its owner. No test failed and no exception was raised, because nothing asserted that a decision remained readable. The class is general: for each state a record can enter, check that some read path returns it. Closed for approvals by 414a222.

risks.title: Coordinator CI notes go stale silently and read as current forever
risks.detail: Three claims in this repo's own docs were false at run start. STATE.md called ca15eb1 'docs-only and unclaimed' when it was 4/4 completed/success at that exact SHA. STATE.md carried PR counters of 28,385 additions / 88 commits when the PR object said 28,409 / 89. BACKLOG.md said 'CI has not yet run on c18bac7' when c18bac7 was 4/4 green. Each was written once at push time and never revisited. A note phrased 'CI has not yet run on X' has no expiry and is indistinguishable, to a later reader, from 'CI failed on X'. Mitigation: name the poll timestamp in any such note, and re-poll any not-yet-observed claim in the next run where that commit is reachable. Polling costs seconds.

risks.summary: A verifier that only checks a seal when the seal exists can be defeated by deleting the seal.
risks.detail: NEX-012 sealed each invocation's verdict in outcome_hash and NEX-012's tests proved that editing the verdict without touching the seal is caught. But verify_chain recomputed the seal only when one was present, so nulling outcome_hash and completed_at together removed the evidence instead of contradicting it, and the chain verified clean. The test attacked the weaker forgery. General rule: for every field a check reads, ask what the check does when that field is absent, and treat absence as a break wherever the state machine says the field must be present. Closed by NEX-018.

risks.summary: Heredocs corrupt or hang in this environment - confirmed a third time, on a commit message.
risks.detail: A `git commit -F -` fed by `cat <<'MSG'` spliced the message into repeated fragments with `iiii...` filler and hung awaiting input; the commit never landed and the tree was intact. Repair: write the message to /tmp with the file editor and use `git commit -F <file>`, then verify line count and grep for the filler string. Prose payloads - commit messages included - never go through a heredoc.

risks.summary: Withholding is safe for security and risky for usefulness: nothing yet reports how often a real input is withheld.
risks.detail: NEX-031 makes an over-cap record-derived value withheld rather than fatal, which is the right failure direction - a legal note must not deny an advisory. But withholding is now the quiet path: excluded_field_names records the fact for the audit trail and nothing counts it. If a real note field routinely exceeds MAX_FIELD_VALUE_LENGTH, every advisory will be computed on a thinner context than the caller believes, and no test or metric will say so. The next observability slice, or the first real decision provider, should surface withheld field names per recommendation. Until then this is a known blind spot, not a defect: the security invariant holds in the safe direction.
